title: Militarism
q: Which development best illustrates militarism before World War I?
opts: European powers signed agreements to dismantle their standing armies and border forts.
Most nations decided to replace their conscription systems with small volunteer forces.
France and Russia signed a treaty to ban the development of new artillery and weaponry.
Britain and Germany competed to build dreadnoughts and expand their strategic war plans.
explanation: Correct: Britain and Germany competed to build dreadnoughts and expand war plans. The naval arms race and offensive planning made military power central to policy and increased mutual fear. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Dreadnought Economy
q: Why did dreadnought production have an economic role?
opts: It maintained employment in heavy industries while expanding strategic naval strength.
It reduced overall military budgets by replacing expensive land-based infantry forces.
It encouraged states to shift industrial investments from manufacturing to local agriculture.
It eliminated the need for overseas merchant trade by securing domestic raw materials.
explanation: Correct: It maintained heavy-industry employment while expanding naval strength. The notes connect shipbuilding to steel and engineering jobs as well as strategic competition. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Alliance Blocs
q: Which pairing correctly identifies the prewar blocs?
opts: Triple Alliance: Germany, France, Russia; Triple Entente: Britain, Austria-Hungary, Italy.
Triple Alliance: Britain, Germany, Italy; Triple Entente: France, Russia, Ottoman Empire.
Triple Alliance: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy; Triple Entente: Britain, France, Russia.
Triple Alliance: France, Britain, Spain; Triple Entente: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Russia.
explanation: Correct: Triple Alliance: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy; Triple Entente: Britain, France, Russia. These were the major alignments, although Italy later left its former partners and joined the Allies. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Alliance Escalation
q: How did alliances widen the 1914 crisis?
opts: They isolated Russia and Serbia from the rest of Europe, keeping the conflict localized.
They placed all military forces of the member nations under a single unified commander.
Mutual defense and counter-mobilization clauses linked the local Austro-Serbian conflict to major powers.
They legally required all signatory states to maintain strict neutrality in regional disputes.
explanation: Correct: Support and counter-mobilization connected an Austro-Serbian conflict to other powers. Russia backed Serbia, Germany backed Austria-Hungary, France supported Russia, and Britain entered after Belgium was invaded. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Nationalism
q: Which situation best shows nationalism destabilizing Europe?
opts: European governments successfully assimilated minor groups and erased regional ethnic identities.
Russia officially rejected Pan-Slavism to avoid diplomatic friction with the Ottoman Empire.
Serbia supported continued Ottoman control over the Balkan region to prevent Austrian expansion.
Slavic groups sought self-determination while Austria-Hungary tried to preserve its multiethnic empire.
explanation: Correct: Slavic peoples sought self-determination while Austria-Hungary tried to preserve its multiethnic empire. Ethnic nationalism threatened empires containing many peoples, especially in the Balkans. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Pan-Slavism
q: Why did Austria-Hungary fear Pan-Slavism?
opts: It could encourage Slavic subjects to seek independence or push for union with Serbia.
It promoted British naval domination by granting Britain access to warm-water ports.
It rapidly industrialized the Russian economy, threatening Austrian agricultural exports.
It supported German efforts to establish direct military control over eastern France.
explanation: Correct: It could encourage Slavic subjects to seek independence or union with Serbia. Russia claimed to protect Slavs, while Austria-Hungary feared separatism among its Slavic populations. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Industrialization
q: How did industrialization increase the scale of war?
opts: It revived medieval tactics by making hand-to-hand combat the dominant form of battle.
It enabled the mass production and rapid transport of weapons, ammunition, and supplies.
It limited the size of national armies because workers were needed to run urban factories.
It reduced conflict by satisfying all raw material demands through synthetic alternatives.
explanation: Correct: It enabled mass production and transport of weapons, ammunition, and supplies. Factories and railroads made mass mobilization and sustained industrial warfare possible. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Imperialism
q: Why did imperialism contribute to World War I?
opts: Imperialism helped secure peace by giving European powers common trade interests in Asia.
Only nations that lacked overseas colonies participated in the initial prewar alliances.
Colonial rivalry raised mutual distrust and eventually carried European conflict around the globe.
The acquisition of colonies made the economic structures of European powers entirely identical.
explanation: Correct: Colonial rivalry increased distrust and carried European conflict around the globe. Empires competed for territory and drew colonial soldiers and resources into the conflict. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: War Plans
q: What danger did rigid plans such as the Schlieffen Plan create?
opts: They encouraged slow negotiations by forcing leaders to consult parliaments before mobilizing.
They prohibited early troop movements and required countries to wait for a declaration of war.
They transferred final military decisions to an international peacekeeping organization.
They rewarded rapid mobilization and offensive action, leaving little time for diplomacy.
explanation: Correct: They rewarded rapid mobilization and offensive action, reducing time for diplomacy. Military timetables made delay appear dangerous and pushed leaders toward escalation. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Schlieffen Plan
q: What problem was the Schlieffen Plan meant to solve?
opts: Germany's risk of fighting a two-front war against France and Russia.
Britain's strategic need to establish military control over Serbia.
Russia's difficulties in maintaining naval access to the Pacific.
Italy's requirement to defend its colonies from Ottoman incursions.
explanation: Correct: Germany's feared two-front war against France and Russia. Germany hoped to defeat France quickly before turning east against slower-mobilizing Russia. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Balkan Wars
q: How did the Balkan Wars raise tension?
opts: They resulted in the transfer of Bosnia to British control, which angered Russia and Germany.
They weakened Ottoman control, sharpened regional territorial disputes, and increased Serbian ambition.
They successfully resolved nationalist grievances, leading to long-term stability in the Balkans.
They led to a secret military alliance between Austria-Hungary and Serbia against the Ottoman Empire.
explanation: Correct: They weakened Ottoman control, sharpened territorial disputes, and increased Serbian ambition. Ottoman retreat left contested lands and a stronger Serbia that alarmed Austria-Hungary. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: The Spark
q: Why is the Sarajevo assassination called a spark rather than the sole cause?
opts: It destroyed the primary military communication networks of all major European nations.
It dissolved existing alliances and forced countries to negotiate new mutual defense treaties.
It activated long-standing militarism, complex alliance webs, nationalism, and colonial rivalries.
It occurred several months after major hostilities had already broken out on the Western Front.
explanation: Correct: It activated deeper militarism, alliances, nationalism, and rivalries. The assassination triggered the July Crisis, but MANIIA conditions made escalation possible. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Gavrilo Princip
q: Who was Gavrilo Princip?
opts: A British admiral who coordinated the naval blockade of Germany.
A German foreign minister who negotiated the alliance with Austria.
A Russian Bolshevik who led early protests against Tsar Nicholas II.
A Bosnian Serb nationalist who assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand.
explanation: Correct: A Bosnian Serb nationalist who assassinated Franz Ferdinand. Princip attacked the Austro-Hungarian heir in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Blank Check
q: What was Germany's blank check?
opts: A promise of full German support for Austria-Hungary's actions during the July Crisis.
An interest-free loan offered to neutral nations to prevent them from joining the Entente.
A treaty signed by Britain ensuring military protection for Belgium in case of invasion.
An ultimatum sent by Russia demanding the immediate demobilization of Austrian forces.
explanation: Correct: A promise of broad support for Austria-Hungary even if action against Serbia widened the crisis. German backing encouraged Vienna to take a hard line while underestimating Russian intervention. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: July Ultimatum
q: Why was Austria-Hungary's ultimatum dangerous?
opts: It was drafted by the United States Senate to isolate Russia from western allies.
Its harsh demands compromised Serbian sovereignty and created a clear pretext for war.
It proposed a partition of the Austro-Hungarian Empire to satisfy Slavic demands.
It ordered an immediate cessation of all military mobilization across Eastern Europe.
explanation: Correct: Its harsh demands challenged Serbian sovereignty and created a pretext for war. Serbia accepted much but rejected intrusive provisions, and Austria-Hungary used that as grounds for war. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Escalation Sequence
q: Which sequence correctly summarizes the July Crisis?
opts: Ultimatum, Russian mobilization, British entry, assassination of the Archduke, German declaration of war.
Russian mobilization, German invasion of France, Sarajevo assassination, British entry, Austrian ultimatum.
Assassination, Austrian ultimatum, war on Serbia, Russian mobilization, invasion of Belgium, British entry.
British entry, German declaration of war, Austrian invasion of Serbia, Russian mobilization, assassination.
explanation: Correct: Assassination, ultimatum, war on Serbia, Russian mobilization, German declarations, Belgium invaded, British entry. The correct chain shows how successive choices transformed a Balkan crisis into a European war. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: British Entry
q: What most directly brought Britain into war against Germany?
opts: Germany's build-up of troops on the Swiss border.
Russia's decision to launch a naval attack on Britain.
Italy's sudden military mobilization against France.
Germany's military invasion of neutral Belgium.
explanation: Correct: Germany's invasion of neutral Belgium. Belgian neutrality and the strategic danger of German control made British nonintervention untenable. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Italy Changes Sides
q: Why did Italy join the Allies in 1915?
opts: It disputed Austrian territory and was promised regional gains by the Allied powers.
It was militarily occupied by British forces and forced to declare war on Germany.
It signed a secret treaty with Russia to establish a joint socialist federation.
It claimed that Germany had violated the terms of their defensive naval alliance.
explanation: Correct: It disputed Austrian territory and was promised gains after judging the Triple Alliance defensive. Italian interests conflicted with Austria-Hungary, and Allied territorial promises encouraged the switch. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: First Marne
q: Why was the First Battle of the Marne significant?
opts: It resulted in the immediate capture of Paris by Ottoman and German forces.
It halted the German advance into France and led to a long Western Front stalemate.
It forced Great Britain to withdraw its troops and declare immediate surrender.
It allowed Russia to capture Berlin and successfully knock Germany out of the war.
explanation: Correct: It stopped Germany's advance and helped produce Western Front stalemate. Germany failed to gain the rapid victory required by its western strategy, and both sides entrenched. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Trench Stalemate
q: Why did trenches produce stalemate?
opts: Industrial military technologies were largely withheld by commanders on both sides.
Trench warfare strategies were applied to naval battles, preventing fleet movement.
Machine guns, artillery, and barbed wire favored protected defenders over exposed attackers.
Cavalry forces were able to cross open fields easily and bypass static defensive lines.
explanation: Correct: Machine guns, artillery, and wire favored protected defenders over exposed attackers. Crossing no man's land under modern fire made offensives costly and gains small. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: No Man's Land
q: What was no man's land?
opts: A naval buffer zone established near Japan.
The demilitarized territory in the Rhineland.
The highly fortified capital city of Russia.
The exposed ground between opposing trenches.
explanation: Correct: The exposed ground between opposing trench systems. It was cratered, wired, and swept by machine-gun and artillery fire. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Total War
q: What best defines total war?
opts: The mobilization of soldiers, civilians, economies, and industry for the war effort.
A conflict that is fought exclusively by professional armies with no civilian impact.
A brief, decisive engagement that is concluded within a single month of fighting.
A war in which governments prohibit the use of media propaganda and censorship.
explanation: Correct: Mobilization of soldiers, civilians, economies, industry, and information for victory. Governments rationed, censored, redirected factories, and treated civilians as part of the war effort. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Women and War
q: What was one lasting effect of women's wartime service?
opts: It legally restricted women from participating in any military support roles.
It strengthened arguments for women's suffrage and broader public economic roles.
It convinced governments that women were unsuited for heavy industrial labor.
It immediately abolished all forms of gender inequality across European society.
explanation: Correct: It strengthened arguments for suffrage and broader public roles. Women's factory, farm, nursing, and communications work challenged older political exclusions. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Verdun
q: Why is Verdun a symbol of attrition?
opts: It was fought entirely by submarines off the coast of northern France.
It convinced the United States to withdraw all economic aid to France.
It resulted in massive casualties without producing any tactical breakthrough.
It was resolved through negotiations and resulted in zero casualties.
explanation: Correct: It caused immense casualties without a decisive breakthrough. Its long struggle and roughly one million combined casualties showed the human cost of wearing down an enemy. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Somme
q: What lesson is associated with the Somme?
opts: Trench fortifications successfully prevented any casualties during the offensive.
The introduction of tanks completely ended the Western Front stalemate in 1916.
The battle demonstrated that modern military actions were best fought in Arabia.
Industrial firepower caused catastrophic casualties for tiny territorial gains.
explanation: Correct: Industrial firepower caused catastrophic losses for limited territorial gains. The offensive demonstrated the mismatch between destructive weapons and weak breakthrough tactics. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Blockade
q: What was the purpose of a naval blockade?
opts: To cut off enemy supplies, food, and commercial trade.
To encourage and facilitate imports for enemy markets.
To ban the use of military submarines in open waters.
To secure abundance of luxury goods for local citizens.
explanation: Correct: To restrict enemy food, raw materials, and trade. Blockades made economic endurance and civilian supply part of total war. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Submarine Warfare
q: Why was unrestricted submarine warfare risky for Germany?
opts: It guaranteed the safety of neutral merchant vessels traveling to British ports.
It threatened neutral shipping and lives, risking United States entry into the war.
It restricted naval operations because submarines could only run close to the shore.
It required written authorization and tactical approval from the British Admiralty.
explanation: Correct: It threatened neutral lives and shipping and could provoke U.S. entry. Attacks without warning endangered American commerce and citizens, generating diplomatic backlash. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Lusitania
q: Why did the sinking of RMS Lusitania matter?
opts: It was a Mexican military vessel carrying vital raw materials to the Central Powers.
It resulted in an international treaty that completely outlawed U-boat warfare.
American deaths turned public opinion against Germany, though the U.S. did not enter yet.
It caused the United States to immediately declare war on Germany the following day.
explanation: Correct: American deaths increased anti-German opinion, though the United States did not enter immediately. The 1915 sinking killed 128 Americans and became an important step in changing public opinion. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Global War
q: Why did the European conflict spread worldwide?
opts: Every overseas colony maintained strict neutrality and refused to participate.
Combat was restricted to European borders, but all trade agreements were cut off.
Only European citizens were permitted to serve in military positions worldwide.
Empires fought in overseas territories and mobilized colonial troops and resources.
explanation: Correct: Empires fought in colonies and mobilized colonial troops, resources, bases, and routes. Imperial networks gave the war worldwide reach and manpower. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Colonial Forces
q: What does the use of imperial troops demonstrate?
opts: The war depended on the human and material resources of global empires.
Colonies remained entirely unaffected by military mobilization plans.
Every overseas colony achieved independence by refusing to support the war.
Colonial populations provided no labor or support for industrial production.
explanation: Correct: The war depended on the human and material resources of global empires. Indian, African, Canadian, Australian, and other forces made the conflict global. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Gallipoli
q: What was the main Allied goal at Gallipoli?
opts: To defend Japanese colonial acquisitions in East Asia from German forces.
To force the straits, weaken the Ottomans, and open a route to Russia.
To launch a land invasion of Mexico to prevent a Central Powers alliance.
To bypass German defenses and capture Berlin by marching through Switzerland.
explanation: Correct: Force the straits, weaken the Ottomans, and open a route toward Russia. Ottoman resistance and difficult terrain turned the attempt into a costly Allied failure. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Japan Enters
q: Why did Japan enter against Germany?
opts: It sought to defend Austria-Hungary's claims in the Pacific from British attacks.
It was bound by treaty obligations to support the Triple Alliance in East Asia.
It used its alliance with Britain and Europe's distraction to seize German territories.
It wanted to restore German control over the Shandong peninsula to maintain stability.
explanation: Correct: It used its British alliance and Europe's distraction to seize German possessions. Japan combined alliance claims with imperial expansion in China and the Pacific. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Twenty-One Demands
q: What did Japan's Twenty-One Demands seek?
opts: The immediate and unconditional independence of all Chinese territories.
The creation of a joint parliament to govern Japan and China together.
The total withdrawal of all Japanese military forces from Shandong.
Greater Japanese political and economic control over the Chinese state.
explanation: Correct: Greater Japanese political and economic influence in China. The demands show Japan exploiting wartime distraction to expand regional power. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Arab Revolt
q: Why did Arabs revolt against Ottoman rule?
opts: They hoped cooperating with the Allies would bring autonomy or independence.
They desired a stronger and more centralized Ottoman administration in the region.
They sought to facilitate German military annexation of the Arabian peninsula.
They wanted to enforce the territorial terms outlined in the Treaty of Versailles.
explanation: Correct: They hoped Allied cooperation would bring autonomy or independence. Wartime promises encouraged revolt, but later imperial settlements disappointed those expectations. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Sykes-Picot
q: What did Sykes-Picot propose?
opts: A secret military alliance between Mexico and Russia to counter American power.
British and French spheres of influence over post-Ottoman Middle Eastern lands.
The immediate establishment of independent Arab sovereign states across the region.
The transfer of military control over India from Great Britain to German forces.
explanation: Correct: British and French spheres of influence in Ottoman Middle Eastern lands. The secret agreement conflicted with Arab hopes and shaped controversial postwar mandates. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Armenian Genocide
q: How did war enable the Armenian Genocide?
opts: The genocide was carried out primarily during high-seas naval battles in the Mediterranean.
The League of Nations quickly intervened and stopped all deportation plans in the region.
Ottoman leaders labeled Armenians a threat and used wartime conditions to deport and kill them.
Allied military forces successfully deployed troops to protect the entire Armenian population.
explanation: Correct: Ottoman leaders labeled Armenians a security threat and used wartime secrecy for deportation and mass killing. Wartime nationalism, fear, and limited outside intervention enabled systematic atrocity. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Russian Vulnerability
q: Why was Russia vulnerable to revolution?
opts: Russia suffered zero military casualties and maintained a fully functioning peacetime economy.
Tsar Nicholas II abdicated early to establish a stable and popular representative democracy.
Russian factory workers and peasant farmers unanimously supported long-term military campaigns.
Military defeats, high casualties, food shortages, and distrust of the Tsar fueled major unrest.
explanation: Correct: Defeats, casualties, shortages, and distrust of Nicholas II intensified existing unrest. War magnified political and economic weakness until confidence in the monarchy collapsed. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Tsar Abdicates
q: What followed Nicholas II's abdication?
opts: Romanov rule ended, and a provisional government competed with soviets for authority.
Vladimir Lenin was crowned as the new tsar, restoring absolute dynastic rule to Russia.
Germany signed an alliance with Russia and officially joined the Triple Entente powers.
A highly stable and peaceful constitutional monarchy was immediately established.
explanation: Correct: Romanov rule ended and a provisional government competed with soviets for authority. The fall of the dynasty created unstable dual power rather than immediate political stability. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Provisional Government
q: Why did the provisional government lose support?
opts: It immediately signed the Treaty of Versailles and paid heavy war reparations to Germany.
It continued the unpopular war and failed to address demands for land, food, and peace.
It successfully delivered peace, redistributed farmland, and secured abundant food supplies.
It dissolved the local soviets and restored absolute autocratic rule under a new dynasty.
explanation: Correct: It continued the unpopular war and failed to solve demands for food, land, and authority. Continued fighting and shortages opened space for Bolshevik promises. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Lenin's Slogan
q: Why was 'Peace, Land, and Bread' effective?
opts: It proposed cutting urban food supplies to feed the frontline soldiers.
It endorsed the secret territorial terms of the Sykes-Picot agreement.
It directly addressed the grievances of soldiers, peasants, and urban workers.
It called for restoring the power of the Tsar and expanding imperial territory.
explanation: Correct: It addressed soldiers, peasants, and hungry urban workers. The slogan directly matched the urgent grievances of major Russian groups. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Bolshevik Policy
q: What major wartime policy followed the Bolshevik seizure of power?
opts: Russia launched a massive offensive on the Eastern Front.
The Tsar formed a new military command with French allies.
Russia negotiated a separate naval treaty with Great Britain.
Lenin sought an immediate armistice and peace with Germany.
explanation: Correct: Lenin sought an immediate armistice and peace with Germany. The Bolsheviks fulfilled their peace promise through negotiations with the Central Powers. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Brest-Litovsk
q: What did Brest-Litovsk accomplish?
opts: Russia withdrew from the war while surrendering major territories to the Central Powers.
The Allies established a joint military occupation over all defeated German colonies.
The Central Powers agreed to a general demobilization along the entire Western Front.
Germany signed a comprehensive peace treaty with all Allied nations to end the war.
explanation: Correct: Russia withdrew from the war while surrendering major territories to the Central Powers. The treaty ended the Eastern Front but imposed a severe territorial price on Russia. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Effect of Russian Exit
q: How did Russian withdrawal affect Germany?
opts: It allowed Germany to secure additional naval bases and reopen the Gallipoli campaign.
Germany shifted troops west for a final offensive before U.S. power fully arrived.
It forced Germany to redeploy its forces to defend against new Allied naval blockades.
It led to a collapse of the French army, guaranteeing an immediate Allied surrender.
explanation: Correct: Germany shifted troops west for a final offensive before U.S. power fully arrived. The closed Eastern Front created a brief German opportunity in 1918. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: U.S. Neutrality
q: Why was the United States initially neutral?
opts: Congress voted to declare war immediately in 1914 to support their European partners.
German diplomats successfully gained veto power over all major U.S. foreign policy.
Many Americans wanted to avoid a distant European war despite ties to the Allies.
The United States was bound by a secret treaty to join the Central Powers' alliance.
explanation: Correct: Many Americans wanted to avoid a distant European war despite ties to the Allies. Distance, tradition, and a divided public delayed entry until 1917. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Zimmermann Telegram
q: What did the Zimmermann Telegram propose?
opts: Great Britain would surrender Canadian territories to the United States to ensure neutrality.
Russia would sign a mutual defense pact with Germany to partition Eastern European lands.
Japan would return the Shandong concession to China to prevent further Western influence.
Mexico ally with Germany against America in exchange for help recovering lost territory.
explanation: Correct: Mexico ally with Germany against America in exchange for help recovering lost territory. Its publication made a European conflict appear to threaten U.S. territory directly. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: U.S. Entry
q: Which combination best explains U.S. entry?
opts: Renewed unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram, reinforced by Lusitania.
The immediate shock of the Franz Ferdinand assassination coupled with the Battle of Verdun.
The threat of a direct naval invasion of the East Coast by German battleships in early 1917.
A formal request from the new Bolshevik government for military aid to defend their capital.
explanation: Correct: Renewed unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram, reinforced by Lusitania. Shipping attacks and the German proposal to Mexico drove the April 1917 declaration. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: American Impact
q: Why did late U.S. entry matter?
opts: It occurred just as Great Britain decided to withdraw its forces from the war.
Fresh troops, supplies, credit, and industry strengthened exhausted Allies.
It shifted the diplomatic balance because America joined the Central Powers.
It allowed the Allies to focus on the Pacific theater where Americans fought.
explanation: Correct: Fresh troops, supplies, credit, and industry strengthened exhausted Allies. American resources shifted the long-term balance after Germany's last offensive failed. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Fourteen Points
q: What was central to Wilson's Fourteen Points?
opts: The complete avoidance of any long-term international political cooperation.
The recognition and consolidation of German hegemony over continental Europe.
Open diplomacy, reduced arms, self-determination, and a League of Nations.
The formal endorsement of secret treaties and new colonial annexations.
explanation: Correct: Open diplomacy, reduced arms, self-determination, and a League of Nations. Wilson hoped to address causes of conflict through a rules-based peace. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Self-Determination
q: What limited postwar self-determination?
opts: The decision to ensure that every ethnic group received a viable state.
It was designed as a policy that applied only to naval military forces.
It resulted in a treaty that restored all pre-war European empires.
It was applied unevenly to colonies and ethnically mixed regions.
explanation: Correct: It was applied unevenly to colonies and ethnically mixed regions. Overlapping populations and imperial interests left many minorities and colonized peoples dissatisfied. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Spring Offensive
q: Why did Germany attack in spring 1918?
opts: To win before American forces arrived in overwhelming numbers.
To assist the Russian military in reclaiming lost eastern territory.
To defend newly acquired German territories in East Asia and Japan.
To enforce the strict conditions outlined in the Treaty of Versailles.
explanation: Correct: To win before American forces arrived in overwhelming numbers. Troops freed from the east gave Germany one final opportunity, but the gamble failed. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Marne 1918
q: Why was stopping Germany near the Marne important in 1918?
opts: It allowed the German army to capture Paris and secure an immediate victory.
It broke the final offensive's momentum and shifted initiative to the Allies.
It led to a successful counter-revolution that restored the Russian tsar.
It forced the Allied commanders to launch the long-delayed Gallipoli campaign.
explanation: Correct: It broke the final offensive's momentum and shifted initiative to the Allies. Allied and American resistance helped turn German advance into retreat. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Meuse-Argonne
q: How did Meuse-Argonne contribute to the end?
opts: It forced the Allied forces to divert resources to attack Japan.
It was fought immediately after the Treaty of Versailles was signed.
It maintained Allied pressure on German forces and communications.
It reopened the Eastern Front and brought Russia back into the war.
explanation: Correct: It maintained Allied pressure on German forces and communications. The September 1918 offensive was part of the advance that exhausted German resistance. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Armistice
q: What happened on November 11, 1918?
opts: The Treaty of Versailles was officially ratified by the United States Senate.
All European nations signed a declaration that officially began World War II.
Russia formally reentered the conflict to assist the remaining Allied powers.
Germany signed an armistice ending combat before the later peace treaty.
explanation: Correct: Germany signed an armistice ending combat before the later peace treaty. An armistice is a cease-fire; the Treaty of Versailles followed in 1919. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Big Four
q: Which pairing correctly identifies the Paris peace leaders?
opts: Wilson (United States), Clemenceau (France), Lloyd George (Britain), and Orlando (Italy)
Wilson (Germany), Clemenceau (Russia), Lloyd George (Serbia), and Orlando (Japan)
Wilson (Britain), Clemenceau (Italy), Lloyd George (United States), and Orlando (France)
Wilson (Austria), Clemenceau (Ottoman Empire), Lloyd George (Germany), and Orlando (Russia)
explanation: Correct: Wilson (United States), Clemenceau (France), Lloyd George (Britain), and Orlando (Italy). The Big Four had different security, territorial, and ideological goals. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Peace Goals
q: Why did Wilson and Clemenceau disagree?
opts: Both leaders opposed all reparations and wanted to quickly rebuild the German economy.
Wilson favored a rules-based peace; Clemenceau emphasized French security and German punishment.
Wilson wanted France to assume complete control over the entire Rhineland region permanently.
Clemenceau wanted a stronger Germany to serve as a military buffer against the Russian Empire.
explanation: Correct: Wilson favored a rules-based peace; Clemenceau emphasized French security and German punishment. France's wartime destruction produced priorities different from Wilson's idealism. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: War Guilt
q: What was the effect of Article 231?
opts: It directly created Bolshevism and sparked immediate revolutions across Europe.
It returned all seized German colonies back to their original imperial rulers.
It assigned German responsibility as a basis for reparations and caused resentment.
It completely denied all responsibility for the outbreak of war on all sides.
explanation: Correct: It assigned German responsibility as a basis for reparations and caused resentment. Germans viewed the clause as humiliating and unjust. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Reparations
q: Why were reparations controversial?
opts: They rewarded Germany with significant postwar industrial development loans.
They required no actual financial payments or resources from any nation.
They targeted neutral nations to fund the reconstruction of Western Europe.
They compensated Allied damage but heavily burdened Germany's weak economy.
explanation: Correct: They compensated Allied damage but burdened Germany's weak economy. The payments became a symbol of a punitive peace and fed instability. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Military Limits
q: Which restriction was imposed on Germany?
opts: A small army, no air force or submarines, and a demilitarized Rhineland.
The right to maintain unlimited armed forces and navy without supervision.
Complete control of all Allied military weapons and domestic industries.
A mandatory political and military alliance with the new Russian state.
explanation: Correct: A small army, no air force or submarines, and a demilitarized Rhineland. The limits sought French security but intensified German resentment. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Territorial Changes
q: Which change resulted from the settlement?
opts: The Ottoman Empire gained control of all territory throughout Arabia.
Alsace-Lorraine returned to France and Poland regained access to the sea.
Germany annexed the entire northern region of France as compensation.
The Austro-Hungarian Empire expanded its borders into the Balkan region.
explanation: Correct: Alsace-Lorraine returned to France and Poland regained access to the sea. The collapse of empires and German losses redrew Europe while creating new minority disputes. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Mandates
q: What was the mandate system?
opts: Germany was granted authority to rule all major territories across the Middle East.
Imperialism officially ended worldwide and all former colonies achieved autonomy.
Victors administered former German and Ottoman lands under League supervision.
All European colonial possessions gained immediate and complete independence worldwide.
explanation: Correct: Victors administered former German and Ottoman lands under League supervision. Many inhabitants regarded mandates as imperial rule under a new name. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: League Purpose
q: What was the League of Nations designed to do?
opts: Coordinate and support future German military conquests.
Directly replace the sovereign national governments of Europe.
Guarantee the practice of secret diplomacy among all members.
Provide collective security and peaceful dispute resolution.
explanation: Correct: Provide collective security and peaceful dispute resolution. Wilson hoped permanent cooperation could deter aggression. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: U.S. Absence
q: Why was the League weakened initially?
opts: The U.S. Senate rejected Versailles, so America never joined.
Both Great Britain and France refused to participate or join.
The League possessed an aggressive and massive standing army.
Germany was allowed to control and direct the organization.
explanation: Correct: The U.S. Senate rejected Versailles, so America never joined. Absence of U.S. economic and military power reduced credibility and enforcement. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Versailles Legacy
q: Why is Versailles linked to later instability?
opts: It successfully unified democratic nations across the European continent.
Humiliation, reparations, and territorial grievances were exploited by extremists.
Germany officially welcomed the terms of the settlement as fair and just.
It completely ended the influence of nationalism in international affairs.
explanation: Correct: Humiliation, reparations, and territorial grievances were exploited by extremists. The treaty did not make another war inevitable, but it created powerful revisionist grievances. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Empire Collapse
q: Which empires collapsed because of war and revolution?
opts: Only the Belgian colonial empire collapsed during the conflict.
None of the major global empires collapsed due to the war.
The German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman, and Russian empires.
The British, French, United States, and Japanese empires.
explanation: Correct: German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman, and Russian empires. Their fall produced new states, mandates, border disputes, and political upheaval. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Cause and Trigger
q: Which interpretation best separates causes from trigger?
opts: The assassination in Sarajevo alone is sufficient to explain imperialism.
All the structural factors of MANIIA only began to develop after 1918.
There were no real long-term structural causes leading to the conflict.
MANIIA created instability; Sarajevo activated it during the July Crisis.
explanation: Correct: MANIIA created instability; Sarajevo activated it during the July Crisis. Long-term structures and short-term decisions must be combined to explain outbreak. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Global Synthesis
q: What do Japan, Arab revolt, colonial troops, and Gallipoli prove?
opts: The war was a global imperial conflict, not only European trench fighting.
Only the Western Front in France played any significant role in the war.
All global colonial territories remained completely neutral and uninvolved.
The Middle East had no strategic or geopolitical value during the conflict.
explanation: Correct: The war was a global imperial conflict, not only European trench fighting. Imperial networks spread combat, bargaining, labor, and resources worldwide. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Russia and America
q: How did Russian exit and U.S. entry pull oppositely?
opts: The United States entry successfully reopened military action in the east.
Russia freed German troops; America added fresh Allied manpower and resources.
Both events combined to strengthen the Russian army's position on the front.
Both actions completely removed Germany's capability to wage war anywhere.
explanation: Correct: Russia freed German troops; America added fresh Allied manpower and resources. Germany gained a short window, but time increasingly favored the Allies. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Wilson and Treaty
q: How did Versailles compare with Wilson's vision?
opts: Wilson demanded unlimited military and economic punishment for Germany without compromise.
The final treaty completely rejected the establishment of a League of Nations structure.
It created the League but added punitive and imperial compromises contrary to much of his program.
It successfully adopted every single one of Wilson's Fourteen Points without modification.
explanation: Correct: It created the League but added punitive and imperial compromises contrary to much of his program. Wilson achieved collective-security machinery but lost many battles over terms and consistency. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: Continuity
q: What shows continuity from imperialism into the postwar order?
opts: All European colonial rule ended immediately and completely across the globe.
European powers withdrew completely and left the Middle East to local rulers.
Japan voluntarily surrendered all its territorial gains and concessions in Asia.
Victors converted former enemy territories into mandates and spheres of influence.
explanation: Correct: Victors converted former enemy territories into mandates and spheres of influence. Old empires fell, but outside control persisted in new legal forms. The other choices conflict with the chronology, actors, or concepts in the course notes.

title: MANIIA Components
q: Select all long-term causes included in MANIIA.
opts: Military and naval buildups
Alliance blocs
Ethnic nationalism
Industrial and imperial rivalry
Successful universal disarmament
explanation: The first four reflect militarism, alliances, nationalism, and industrialization/imperialism. Europe lacked effective universal disarmament.

title: Escalation Decisions
q: Select all decisions that widened the July Crisis.
opts: Germany gave Austria-Hungary broad support.
Austria-Hungary issued a harsh ultimatum and attacked Serbia.
Russia mobilized in support of Serbia.
Germany invaded neutral Belgium.
Every power demobilized under binding mediation.
correct: Austria-Hungary issued a harsh ultimatum and attacked Serbia.
Russia mobilized in support of Serbia.
explanation: The first four steps expanded the crisis or drew in another power; successful general demobilization did not occur.

title: Total War Home Front
q: Select all features of total war.
opts: Rationing
Propaganda and censorship
Women in war industries and support roles
Civilian production redirected to military needs
Complete civilian separation from war
correct: Women in war industries and support roles
Civilian production redirected to military needs
explanation: Total war mobilized economies, information, and civilians. It erased rather than preserved civilian separation.

title: Industrial Warfare
q: Select all technologies that increased battlefield destruction.
opts: Machine guns
Heavy artillery
Poison gas
Barbed wire
A universal production ban
explanation: The first four strengthened industrial firepower and defensive systems. No universal production ban restrained the belligerents.

title: Japan in the War
q: Select all actions associated with Japan.
opts: Demanded German concessions in East Asia
Seized German possessions
Issued the Twenty-One Demands to China
Expanded influence while Europe was distracted
Joined Germany against Britain
correct: Demanded German concessions in East Asia
Issued the Twenty-One Demands to China
Expanded influence while Europe was distracted
explanation: Japan fought against Germany, seized possessions, and pressured China; it did not join Germany against Britain.

title: Global Scope
q: Select all evidence that the war extended beyond France and Belgium.
opts: Gallipoli
Japan's Pacific seizures
The Arab Revolt
Colonial troops and resources
No military activity outside Western Europe
explanation: The first four demonstrate campaigns and mobilization across imperial regions; the final statement is false.

title: Russian Exit Factors
q: Select all factors driving Russia from the war.
opts: Military failures and casualties
Food shortages and economic breakdown
Collapse of confidence in Nicholas II
Bolshevik promises of peace
A decisive Russian victory
correct: Collapse of confidence in Nicholas II
explanation: Defeat, scarcity, political collapse, and Bolshevik policy pushed withdrawal. Russia had not won decisively.

title: U.S. Entry Factors
q: Select all factors contributing to U.S. entry.
opts: Unrestricted submarine warfare
Zimmermann Telegram
American deaths in attacks such as Lusitania
Growing ties to the Allied cause
A German guarantee protecting all shipping
correct: American deaths in attacks such as Lusitania
Growing ties to the Allied cause
explanation: The first four shifted policy and opinion toward war; a reliable shipping guarantee would have reduced tension.

title: German Armistice
q: Select all conditions pushing Germany toward an armistice.
opts: Failure of the final offensive
Growing American strength
Allied counteroffensives
Collapse of Germany's partners
German conquest of France
explanation: Germany's gamble failed while Allied strength rose and its partners collapsed. France had not been conquered.

title: Versailles Terms
q: Select all terms associated with Versailles.
opts: War responsibility placed on Germany
Reparations
German military and territorial restrictions
League of Nations
German annexation of France
explanation: The first four were central features of the Treaty of Versailles: the war-guilt clause, reparations, military restrictions, and German territorial losses. Germany did not annex France; instead, Alsace-Lorraine was returned to France, making that option historically incorrect.

title: Postwar Consequences
q: Select all major consequences of World War I.
opts: Collapse of four empires
New states and disputed borders
Expanded women's political claims
German resentment of the settlement
Permanent resolution of colonial conflict
explanation: The first four consequences reshaped the postwar world through political collapse, redrawn borders, economic disruption, and social loss. National and colonial disputes did not disappear after 1918; many continued or intensified because the peace settlement left major grievances unresolved.

title: Chronology
q: Select all events that occurred before the November 11, 1918 armistice.
opts: Assassination of Franz Ferdinand
Zimmermann Telegram
Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
Meuse-Argonne Offensive
Treaty of Versailles
explanation: The first four events occurred between the outbreak of war in 1914 and the autumn of 1918, before the armistice ended the fighting on November 11. The Treaty of Versailles was signed later, on June 28, 1919, so it cannot be selected as a pre-armistice event.
